patches.old: - **Wider CI** = less precision = smaller sample, higher variability, or lower confidence level.
patches.new: - **Wider CI** = less precision = smaller sample, higher variability, or a **higher** confidence level. Note the direction carefully: demanding more confidence means casting a wider net, so a 99% CI is always wider than a 95% CI computed from the same data, and a 90% CI is narrower than both.

patches.old: Originally observed in productivity studies at the Hawthorne Works factory in the 1920s, it is a major concern in behavioral research.
patches.new: It takes its name from productivity studies run at the Hawthorne Works factory in the 1920s, although the original claim has not survived scrutiny — when the long-lost illumination data were recovered and analysed, there was no systematic jump in productivity whenever the lighting was changed. The underlying phenomenon, usually called **reactivity**, is nonetheless real and well documented in behavioural research; treat “Hawthorne effect” as the conventional name for it rather than as a reference to a well-established finding.

sources.title: Levitt & List, “Was There Really a Hawthorne Effect at the Hawthorne Plant?” (NBER w15016)

visual.title: Two ways to be wrong, and which way each bias pushes
visual.alt: A two-by-two decision table with the truth about the null hypothesis in the columns and the researcher's decision in the rows, marking Type I error with probability alpha, Type II error with probability beta, and the two correct cells including power as one minus beta; a panel listing what raises power and a panel giving the confidence-interval readings for differences and ratios along with what makes an interval wider; and a panel sorting the research biases into those that inflate an effect and those that hide or shrink it.
visual.caption: Tightening alpha only trades one error for the other — a larger sample is the only thing that shrinks both.
